{{No footnotes|date=July 2025}}{{Short description|Property of group subsets (mathematics)}}
In [[mathematics]], a nonempty subset {{mvar|S}} of a [[Group (mathematics)|group]] {{mvar|G}} is said to be '''symmetric''' if it contains the [[Inverse element|inverses]] of all of its elements.

== Definition ==

In [[Set-builder notation|set notation]] a subset <math>S</math> of a group <math>G</math> is called {{em|symmetric}} if whenever <math>s \in S</math> then the inverse of <math>s</math> also belongs to <math>S.</math> 
So if <math>G</math> is written multiplicatively then <math>S</math> is symmetric if and only if <math>S = S^{-1}</math> where <math>S^{-1} := \left\{ s^{-1} : s \in S \right\}.</math> 
If <math>G</math> is written additively then <math>S</math> is symmetric if and only if <math>S = - S</math> where <math>- S := \{- s : s \in S\}.</math>

If <math>S</math> is a subset of a [[vector space]] then <math>S</math> is said to be a {{em|symmetric set}} if it is symmetric with respect to the [[additive group]] structure of the vector space; that is, if <math>S = - S,</math> which happens if and only if <math>- S \subseteq S.</math>  The {{em|symmetric hull}} of a subset <math>S</math> is the smallest symmetric set containing <math>S,</math> and it is equal to <math>S \cup - S.</math> The largest symmetric set contained in <math>S</math> is <math>S \cap - S.</math>

== Sufficient conditions ==

Arbitrary [[Union (set theory)|unions]] and [[Intersection (set theory)|intersections]] of symmetric sets are symmetric.

Any [[Linear subspace|vector subspace]] in a vector space is a symmetric set.

== Examples ==

In <math>\R,</math> examples of symmetric sets are intervals of the type <math>(-k, k)</math> with <math>k > 0,</math> and the sets <math>\Z</math> and <math>(-1, 1).</math>

If <math>S</math> is any subset of a group, then <math>S \cup S^{-1}</math> and <math>S \cap S^{-1}</math> are symmetric sets. 

Any [[Balanced set|balanced subset]] of a real or complex [[vector space]] is symmetric.
